cards.q: Which cell is the final common pathway, the last neuron every motor command must pass through on its way to skeletal muscle?
cards.a: The alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn of the spinal cord.
options: The alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
The pyramidal cell in the primary motor cortex
The reticulospinal neuron in the brainstem reticular formation
The interneuron in the intermediate spinal gray matter
cards.explanation: Every command, whether it comes from the cortex, the brainstem, or a spinal reflex, converges on the alpha motor neuron, which is why it is called the final common pathway. The cortical pyramidal cell and the reticulospinal neuron are upper levels of the hierarchy and reach muscle only by driving that alpha motor neuron. Spinal interneurons shape the command but still hand it off to the alpha motor neuron rather than reaching the muscle themselves.

cards.q: Which level of the motor hierarchy selects the goal of a voluntary movement and plans the strategy for reaching it?
cards.a: The association and premotor areas of the cortex.
options: The spinal cord interneuron pools
The association and premotor areas of the cortex
The brainstem reticular formation
The alpha motor neurons of the ventral horn
cards.explanation: The highest level of the hierarchy decides what to do and roughly how to do it, and that planning work belongs to the prefrontal association cortex together with the premotor and supplementary motor areas. The brainstem sets postural background rather than choosing the goal. Spinal interneurons and alpha motor neurons execute whatever command arrives; they carry out the plan and do not form it.

cards.q: What is the main contribution of the brainstem level to a voluntary movement?
cards.a: It sets postural tone and balance so the movement has a stable base.
options: It generates the action potential in the muscle fiber itself
It chooses which object the movement will be aimed at
It sets postural tone and balance so the movement has a stable base
It stores the memory of how the movement felt last time
cards.explanation: Brainstem centers act mostly through the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts on axial and proximal muscles, holding the trunk and limb girdles steady so the hand can be moved accurately. Choosing the target is cortical planning. The muscle action potential is generated at the neuromuscular junction by the lower motor neuron. Motor memory is built in cortical and cerebellar circuits, not in the postural brainstem pathways.

cards.q: Which level of the motor hierarchy carries out the monosynaptic stretch reflex?
cards.a: The spinal cord.
options: The primary motor cortex
The cerebellum
The midbrain
The spinal cord
cards.explanation: The stretch reflex is a single synapse between the Ia afferent from the muscle spindle and the alpha motor neuron supplying the same muscle, and both cells are in the spinal cord, so no higher level is required for the response to occur. The primary motor cortex and midbrain modulate the gain of that reflex but are not part of the loop. The cerebellum monitors the movement and adjusts later commands rather than producing the reflex contraction.

cards.q: Where do the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts originate?
cards.a: In the brainstem.
options: In the brainstem
In the primary motor cortex
In the dorsal root ganglia
In the basal ganglia
cards.explanation: Both are brainstem pathways: the vestibulospinal tract arises from the vestibular nuclei and the reticulospinal tracts from the reticular formation, and together they form the middle level of the hierarchy for posture and gross proximal control. Corticospinal fibers, not these tracts, arise in the primary motor cortex. The dorsal root ganglia hold sensory cell bodies and send nothing down the cord. The basal ganglia have no direct descending projection to the spinal cord at all.

cards.q: What does the primary motor cortex specify when it issues a command for a voluntary movement?
cards.a: The force and direction of the movement to be executed.
options: Whether the movement is worth making at all
The force and direction of the movement to be executed
The resting length of the muscle spindle
The concentration of acetylcholine stored in the axon terminal
cards.explanation: Primary motor cortex output encodes execution parameters, chiefly how much force to produce and in what direction to move, and it distributes those parameters to the correct motor neuron pools. Deciding whether a movement is worth making is a higher planning and motivational function. Spindle resting length is set by gamma motor neurons at the spinal level. Transmitter stores in the terminal are a property of the lower motor neuron, not something the cortex specifies.

cards.q: Where are the central pattern generators that produce the basic rhythm of walking?
cards.a: In circuits of the spinal cord.
options: In the primary motor cortex
In the thalamus
In circuits of the spinal cord
In the muscle spindle itself
cards.explanation: Central pattern generators are networks of spinal interneurons that alternate flexor and extensor activity on their own, which is why the basic stepping rhythm does not have to be composed step by step by the brain. The cortex starts, stops, and steers walking but does not generate the rhythm. The thalamus is a relay to cortex with no rhythm-generating role for locomotion. The spindle is a sensory receptor and can modulate the pattern but cannot create it.

cards.q: What is a motor unit?
cards.a: One alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates.
options: One muscle fiber and all the motor neurons that reach it
One upper motor neuron and the lower motor neuron it drives
One whole muscle and the tendon that attaches it to bone
One alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates
cards.explanation: A motor unit is one lower motor neuron plus its entire family of muscle fibers, so when that neuron fires, every fiber in the unit contracts together. The reverse arrangement is not how skeletal muscle is wired, since each mature fiber is innervated by only one motor neuron. A whole muscle contains many motor units drawn from many motor neurons. The upper and lower motor neuron pair describes the descending pathway, not the unit of muscle output.

cards.q: A patient has a complete spinal cord transection at T10. Several months later, what happens to the patellar tendon reflex, which is organized at L2 to L4?
cards.a: It is still present, because the reflex arc below the lesion is intact.
options: It is still present, because the reflex arc below the lesion is intact
It is permanently abolished, because the cord below the lesion is disconnected from the brain
It is still present, but only if the patient concentrates on the leg
It is abolished, because the sensory neuron dies once descending input is lost
cards.explanation: The reflex is a spinal loop from the Ia afferent to the alpha motor neuron at L2 to L4, and none of those elements are damaged by a lesion three segments higher, so tapping the tendon still produces a knee jerk once spinal shock has resolved. Losing the connection to the brain removes voluntary control and descending modulation, not the loop itself. Attention cannot substitute for a pathway that has been cut. The sensory neuron has its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion and survives the cord lesion.

cards.q: Damage limited to the brainstem reticulospinal and vestibulospinal pathways would be expected to impair which movements the most?
cards.a: Holding the trunk upright and keeping balance while standing.
options: Buttoning a shirt with the fingertips
Holding the trunk upright and keeping balance while standing
Detecting a light touch on the sole of the foot while standing
Deciding which of two objects to pick up
cards.explanation: These brainstem pathways run to axial and proximal muscle pools, so losing them costs postural tone and balance while leaving distal dexterity comparatively intact. Fine finger movement depends on the lateral corticospinal tract, which is a separate pathway. Light touch is a sensory function carried by ascending tracts. Choosing between objects is a cortical planning function above the brainstem level.

cards.q: A person reaches for a coffee cup. Which sequence follows the motor hierarchy from planning to contraction?
cards.a: Association cortex, then primary motor cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then muscle.
options: Primary motor cortex, then association cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then muscle
Alpha motor neuron, then primary motor cortex, then association cortex, then muscle
Association cortex, then primary motor cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then muscle
Association cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then primary motor cortex, then muscle
cards.explanation: The hierarchy runs from the level that sets the goal down to the level that produces force: association and premotor cortex plan the reach, the primary motor cortex specifies the execution parameters, the alpha motor neuron delivers the command, and the muscle contracts. Putting the primary motor cortex before the association cortex reverses planning and execution. The sequences that place the alpha motor neuron in the middle or at the start invert the hierarchy, since the final common pathway cannot precede the levels that command it.

cards.q: Recording from a person about to make a self-initiated movement, which area shows activity earliest, before the movement begins?
cards.a: The supplementary motor and premotor areas.
options: The muscle spindles of the antagonist muscle
The ventral horn alpha motor neurons
The neuromuscular junctions of the muscle involved
The supplementary motor and premotor areas
cards.explanation: Planning precedes execution, so the supplementary motor and premotor areas become active first, well before the command reaches the cord. Alpha motor neurons and neuromuscular junctions fire only once the descending command arrives, so they are late in the sequence, not early. Spindles in the antagonist respond to stretch that occurs after the movement has already started, making them the last of these to change.

cards.q: A small stroke destroys only the hand region of the left primary motor cortex. What is the expected pattern of loss?
cards.a: Loss of independent finger movements on the right, with sitting posture preserved.
options: Loss of independent finger movements on the right, with sitting posture preserved
Loss of all movement and all sensation on the right side of the body
Loss of postural tone in the trunk, with finger movements preserved
Loss of the ability to feel the position of the right hand, with movement preserved
cards.explanation: The primary motor cortex hand area supplies the corticospinal drive for fractionated finger movement, and the lesion is small and confined, so the deficit is a contralateral hand deficit while brainstem pathways keep trunk posture normal. A loss of everything on one side would require a much larger lesion involving sensory pathways as well. Losing trunk tone while sparing the fingers is the pattern of a brainstem pathway lesion, not a cortical hand area lesion. Position sense travels in ascending sensory tracts and is not lost from a purely motor cortical lesion.

cards.q: Why can a spinal reflex correct a stumble faster than a cortical response can?
cards.a: The reflex loop is short and uses very few synapses.
options: Sensory axons conduct faster on the way to the cord than on the way to the brain
The reflex loop is short and uses very few synapses
The spinal cord uses a faster neurotransmitter than the cortex does
Reflex signals travel through gap junctions rather than chemical synapses
cards.explanation: Latency comes mostly from distance and from synaptic delay, and a spinal loop keeps both small, so the correction begins tens of milliseconds before a cortical route could deliver a command. The same afferent fiber carries the signal in both cases, so conduction velocity in the afferent is not the difference. Transmitter identity does not differ in a way that explains the timing, and glutamate is used at both levels. Spinal reflex synapses are chemical, not electrical.

cards.q: In an experimental preparation, the brainstem is separated from the cortex but left connected to the spinal cord. Extensor tone in the limbs increases markedly. What does this tell you about the normal role of the higher level?
cards.a: Cortical input normally restrains brainstem excitatory drive to extensor motor neurons.
options: The brainstem normally has no influence on muscle tone in the limbs
Cortical input normally supplies all of the excitation reaching extensor motor neurons
Cortical input normally restrains brainstem excitatory drive to extensor motor neurons
The spinal cord normally generates extensor tone without any descending input
cards.explanation: If tone rises when the higher level is removed, the higher level must have been holding the lower level in check, so cortical influence normally damps the excitatory reticulospinal and vestibulospinal drive to extensors. If the cortex supplied the excitation, removing it would lower tone rather than raise it. The result also shows directly that the brainstem does influence limb tone. The isolated cord immediately after separation is flaccid, so the cord alone does not generate this tone.

cards.q: Weeks after a complete thoracic cord transection, an animal supported on a moving treadmill produces alternating stepping in the hindlimbs but never begins walking on its own. What does this pattern show about the two levels involved?
cards.a: Spinal circuits still generate the stepping rhythm, but the descending command that starts and steers walking is gone.
options: Spinal circuits have taken over the planning functions normally performed by the cortex
The stepping rhythm is generated in the brainstem and still reaches the hindlimbs through the few fibers that survived
The stepping is a single stretch reflex repeated over and over by the moving belt
Spinal circuits still generate the stepping rhythm, but the descending command that starts and steers walking is gone
cards.explanation: Two facts have to be reconciled: the rhythm is present, so its generator lies below the cut in the spinal cord, and initiation is absent, so the command to start comes from above the cut. That is the definition of a spinal central pattern generator driven by descending initiation. Nothing crosses a complete transection, so a brainstem rhythm could not reach the hindlimbs. A repeated stretch reflex could not produce the correct flexor and extensor alternation with proper timing. Isolated spinal circuits gain no planning ability; they lost their access to the plan.

cards.q: A stroke destroys the leg area of the right primary motor cortex. Six weeks later, what is the expected combination of voluntary dorsiflexion and ankle stretch reflex on the left?
cards.a: Voluntary dorsiflexion is lost or very weak, and the ankle reflex is exaggerated.
options: Voluntary dorsiflexion is lost or very weak, and the ankle reflex is exaggerated
Voluntary dorsiflexion is lost or very weak, and the ankle reflex is absent
Voluntary dorsiflexion is preserved, and the ankle reflex is exaggerated
Both voluntary dorsiflexion and the ankle reflex are normal by six weeks
cards.explanation: Two separate consequences follow from one lesion. The descending command for voluntary movement is gone, so dorsiflexion to command fails on the opposite side, and the spinal reflex arc is intact but no longer damped by descending input, so the stretch reflex is released and becomes brisk. Preserved voluntary movement would require the descending pathway to be working. An absent reflex would mean the spinal arc itself was damaged, which a cortical lesion does not do. Recovery to fully normal in six weeks is not expected after destruction of the cortical leg area.

cards.q: A person walking on a path sees a low branch and lifts the leg higher to step over it. Which description best captures how the levels of the hierarchy share this task?
cards.a: Cortex modifies the timing and size of the step while spinal circuits keep producing the walking rhythm.
options: The spinal cord detects the branch and raises the leg without involving the brain
Cortex modifies the timing and size of the step while spinal circuits keep producing the walking rhythm
The cortex takes over completely and generates each individual muscle contraction of the step cycle
The brainstem detects the branch visually and issues the command to lift the leg
cards.explanation: Visual information about the obstacle reaches cortex, which adjusts the ongoing pattern by increasing flexion at the right moment, while the spinal pattern generator continues to supply the underlying alternation. The cord has no access to vision, so it cannot detect the branch. If cortex generated every contraction, walking would not survive loss of cortical input, which it partly does. The brainstem contributes postural adjustment during the step but is not the visual processor issuing the modification.

cards.q: A patient sits with normal posture, has normal tendon reflexes in both arms, and withdraws the hand promptly from a hot surface, yet cannot lift that arm when asked to. Which level of the hierarchy is most likely damaged?
cards.a: The cortical level that issues voluntary commands.
options: The muscle itself
The alpha motor neurons supplying the arm
The cortical level that issues voluntary commands
The sensory afferents entering the cord from the arm
cards.explanation: Work backward from what still functions. Reflex withdrawal and normal tendon reflexes prove that the afferents, the spinal circuitry, the alpha motor neurons, and the muscle can all produce contraction, so the failure is specific to movement on command, which points to the level that generates voluntary commands. Damaged muscle or damaged alpha motor neurons would weaken the reflex contraction as well. Damaged afferents would blunt the withdrawal and the tendon reflexes rather than sparing them.

cards.q: Where are the cell bodies of the neurons that begin the corticospinal pathway?
cards.a: In the primary motor cortex of the precentral gyrus.
options: In the vestibular nuclei of the brainstem
In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
In the primary motor cortex of the precentral gyrus
cards.explanation: Most corticospinal axons arise from large pyramidal cells in layer V of the precentral gyrus, with contributions from nearby premotor and parietal areas. The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex and sends no corticospinal motor output. The ventral horn holds the lower motor neurons where this pathway ends, not where it starts. The vestibular nuclei give rise to the vestibulospinal tract, a separate brainstem pathway.

cards.q: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross the midline?
cards.a: In the pyramids of the medulla.
options: In the pyramids of the medulla
In the internal capsule
In the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
At the level of the spinal segment where it ends
cards.explanation: The pyramidal decussation sits at the junction of the medulla and the spinal cord, and it is the reason a cortical lesion produces weakness on the opposite side of the body. The internal capsule and cerebral peduncle both carry these fibers, but on their original side, before any crossing. Crossing at the segment of termination describes the smaller anterior corticospinal tract, not the lateral tract.

cards.q: About what fraction of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation?
cards.a: About 90 percent.
options: About 50 percent
About 90 percent
About 10 percent
All of them
cards.explanation: Roughly 90 percent of the fibers cross in the medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract, and the remaining tenth continue uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract. Ten percent is the size of the uncrossed group, not the crossed one. A half and half split would not produce the strongly contralateral weakness seen after a cortical lesion. Saying all fibers cross ignores the anterior tract entirely.

cards.q: Which muscles does the anterior corticospinal tract mainly serve?
cards.a: Axial and proximal muscles of the trunk and shoulder girdle.
options: The small muscles of the hand and foot
The muscles that move the eyes
Axial and proximal muscles of the trunk and shoulder girdle
The smooth muscle in the walls of blood vessels in the limbs
cards.explanation: The uncrossed anterior tract stays near the midline of the cord and ends on motor pools for axial and proximal muscles, contributing to posture and gross positioning. Fine control of the hand and foot is the job of the crossed lateral tract. Eye muscles are driven by cranial nerve nuclei through corticobulbar and brainstem gaze pathways. Vascular smooth muscle is under autonomic control and receives no corticospinal input.

cards.q: Through which part of the internal capsule do corticospinal fibers descend?
cards.a: The posterior limb.
options: The anterior limb
They bypass the internal capsule entirely
The genu only
The posterior limb
cards.explanation: Corticospinal fibers are packed into the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which is why a small infarct there can weaken an entire half of the body. The anterior limb carries frontopontine and thalamic connections rather than the limb motor fibers. The genu carries corticobulbar fibers heading for cranial nerve nuclei. Every corticospinal axon passes through the capsule on its way from the corona radiata to the brainstem.

cards.q: Which midbrain structure carries corticospinal fibers on their way toward the spinal cord?
cards.a: The cerebral peduncle.
options: The cerebral peduncle
The red nucleus
The substantia nigra
The superior colliculus
cards.explanation: The cerebral peduncle is the massive fiber bundle on the ventral surface of the midbrain, and the corticospinal fibers occupy its middle portion as they pass through. The superior colliculus handles visual orienting reflexes. The red nucleus gives rise to the rubrospinal tract, which is a separate descending pathway. The substantia nigra belongs to the basal ganglia circuitry and sends its output to the striatum, not to the cord.

cards.q: Where do lateral corticospinal tract axons end?
cards.a: On alpha motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord.
options: On sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion
On alpha motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
Directly on the motor end plate of the skeletal muscle fiber itself
On second order sensory neurons in the dorsal column nuclei of the medulla
cards.explanation: The descending axon ends in the spinal gray matter, contacting the alpha motor neuron directly in the case of hand muscles and contacting interneurons for many other pools. It never reaches muscle itself, since the lower motor neuron axon covers that last stretch to the end plate. Dorsal root ganglion cells are sensory and receive no corticospinal ending. The dorsal column nuclei are relay stations on the ascending sensory route.

cards.q: How many neurons are in series between the primary motor cortex and a skeletal muscle fiber in the corticospinal pathway?
cards.a: Two.
options: Four
One
Two
Three
cards.explanation: The pathway uses an upper motor neuron running from cortex to the spinal gray matter and a lower motor neuron running from the ventral horn to the muscle, so two cells span the whole distance. One neuron would mean a cortical cell reaching the muscle directly, which does not occur. Three or four would suit a sensory pathway with several relays, but the motor route is deliberately short to keep conduction fast.

cards.q: A lesion destroys the hand region of the left primary motor cortex. Which hand becomes weak?
cards.a: The right hand, because the tract crosses below the lesion.
options: Neither hand, because brainstem pathways take over hand control
The left hand, because the tract has already crossed above the lesion
Both hands equally, because the tract supplies both sides
The right hand, because the tract crosses below the lesion
cards.explanation: The decussation is in the medulla, well below the cortex, so fibers leaving the left cortex have not yet crossed and will end up serving the right side of the body. The left hand would be weak only if the lesion sat below the crossing. Bilateral weakness would require the tract to supply both sides equally, which the small uncrossed anterior tract does only for axial muscles. Brainstem pathways cannot substitute for fine hand control.

cards.q: A lesion damages the right medullary pyramid, just above the pyramidal decussation. Where is the resulting weakness?
cards.a: On the left side of the body.
options: On the left side of the body
On the right side of the body
On both sides of the body below the neck
In the right arm and the left leg
cards.explanation: Fibers in the right pyramid have not crossed yet, and they are destined to cross a few millimeters lower and supply the left side, so the weakness appears contralateral to the lesion. Weakness on the same side would require a lesion below the decussation, in the lateral corticospinal tract of the cord. A one-sided pyramid lesion cannot weaken both sides. A split pattern with one arm and the opposite leg does not match a tract that crosses all at one point.

cards.q: A lesion damages the right lateral corticospinal tract at spinal level C5. Where is the weakness?
cards.a: In the right arm and right leg, on the same side as the lesion.
options: In the left arm and left leg, on the side opposite the lesion
In the right arm and right leg, on the same side as the lesion
In both arms but neither leg
In the right arm only, with the right leg spared
cards.explanation: By C5 these fibers have already crossed in the medulla, so the tract on the right side of the cord is serving right sided muscles and a lesion there produces ipsilateral weakness below the level. Contralateral weakness is the pattern for a lesion above the decussation. One-sided cord damage does not affect both arms. Fibers for the leg travel in the same tract and are cut too, so the leg is not spared.

cards.q: A small infarct in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule interrupts a dense bundle of corticospinal fibers. What deficit is expected?
cards.a: Weakness of the right arm and right leg together.
options: Weakness of the right hand alone
Weakness of the left arm and left leg together
Weakness of the right arm and right leg together
Weakness confined to the muscles of the trunk
cards.explanation: Fibers from the whole body map are squeezed into a small volume in the capsule, so a small lesion there strikes arm and leg fibers at once and produces contralateral weakness of the whole side. Weakness of the hand alone is the signature of a small lesion up in the cortex, where the body map is spread out. Left sided weakness would require a lesion below the decussation or on the right. Trunk muscles receive substantial uncrossed input and are the least affected.

cards.q: If the lateral corticospinal tract alone were selectively interrupted, which task would suffer the most?
cards.a: Picking up a small coin with the fingertips.
options: Standing still with the eyes open
Breathing quietly at rest
Holding the head upright while seated
Picking up a small coin with the fingertips
cards.explanation: The lateral tract carries the fractionated commands that let individual fingers move independently, so precision grip is what fails first and most completely. Standing still and holding the head up rely on axial and proximal pools driven by brainstem pathways and the anterior corticospinal tract. Quiet breathing is generated by brainstem respiratory centers and does not need the corticospinal tract at all.

cards.q: The leg region of the primary motor cortex sits on the medial surface of the hemisphere. A stroke that damages only that medial strip on the right would produce what?
cards.a: Weakness of the left leg with relative sparing of the left hand.
options: Weakness of the left leg with relative sparing of the left hand
Weakness of the right leg with relative sparing of the right hand
Weakness of the left hand with relative sparing of the left leg
Equal weakness of the left arm, leg, and face
cards.explanation: The motor homunculus places the leg at the medial edge and the hand on the lateral convexity, so a medial lesion takes out leg fibers and largely spares hand fibers, and the decussation then places the deficit on the opposite side. Hand weakness with a spared leg would follow a lateral convexity lesion instead. Right sided weakness would require the lesion to be on the left. Equal involvement of arm, leg, and face fits a capsular lesion where all the fibers are packed together.

cards.q: Which structure would a corticospinal axon reach first after leaving the internal capsule?
cards.a: The cerebral peduncle of the midbrain.
options: The pyramid of the medulla
The cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
The lateral corticospinal tract of the cord
The ventral horn of the cervical cord
cards.explanation: The route runs downward through the brainstem in order, so the midbrain peduncle comes next, then the basilar pons, then the medullary pyramid, then the cord. The pyramid is two brainstem levels further along. The lateral corticospinal tract exists only after the fibers have crossed in the medulla. The ventral horn is the destination at the far end of the pathway.

cards.q: A patient has weakness of the right arm and leg, and the tongue deviates toward the left when protruded, indicating a left hypoglossal nerve problem. Where must the single lesion sit relative to the pyramidal decussation?
cards.a: In the left medulla, above the decussation.
options: In the left spinal cord, below the decussation
In the right medulla, above the decussation
In the left medulla, above the decussation
In the right cerebral peduncle, above the decussation
cards.explanation: Two findings have to be satisfied at once. The hypoglossal nerve does not cross, so a left tongue sign places the lesion on the left, and the body weakness on the right then requires the corticospinal fibers to still be uncrossed, which puts the lesion above the decussation on the left. A right sided lesion would weaken the left body and the right tongue. A lesion below the decussation would give left sided weakness on the left. The peduncle is far above the hypoglossal nucleus, so it cannot explain the tongue finding.

cards.q: A cord injury damages the right half of the spinal cord at T6. Trace the corticospinal fibers to predict which leg is weak and why.
cards.a: The right leg, because those fibers crossed in the medulla and now run on the right side of the cord.
options: The left leg, because corticospinal fibers cross the midline at the spinal segment where they end
Neither leg, because the anterior corticospinal tract takes over leg control
Both legs, because each lateral tract sends branches to both sides of the cord
The right leg, because those fibers crossed in the medulla and now run on the right side of the cord
cards.explanation: Follow the fibers: axons from the left cortex crossed in the medulla, descended in the right lateral corticospinal tract, and are heading for right sided motor neurons, so cutting the right half of the cord at T6 weakens the right leg. Crossing at the segment of termination applies only to the small anterior tract, and it serves axial muscles. The lateral tract does not send branches across the midline of the cord. The anterior tract is too small and too axial to preserve leg strength.

cards.q: Two patients each have a right sided lesion: one in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the other in the lateral corticospinal tract at C7. Which statement about the side of weakness is correct?
cards.a: The capsular lesion weakens the left side, and the C7 lesion weakens the right side.
options: The capsular lesion weakens the left side, and the C7 lesion weakens the right side
The capsular lesion weakens the right side, and the C7 lesion weakens the left side
Both lesions weaken the right side, since both are on the right
Both lesions weaken the left side, since corticospinal fibers always cross
cards.explanation: The side of weakness depends entirely on whether the lesion sits above or below the pyramidal decussation. The capsule is above it, so those fibers have not crossed and the deficit appears on the left, while C7 is below it, so those fibers already crossed and the deficit stays on the right. Assuming the fibers have always crossed ignores the capsule, and assuming the deficit always matches the side of the lesion ignores the decussation altogether. The reversed pairing gets both levels backward.

cards.q: After a lesion confined to the left medullary pyramid, which combination of findings on the right side is expected?
cards.a: Fine finger movements are severely impaired while sitting posture and trunk control are largely preserved.
options: Sitting posture and trunk control collapse completely while fine finger movements remain entirely accurate
Fine finger movements are severely impaired while sitting posture and trunk control are largely preserved
All voluntary and reflex movement is permanently abolished
Muscle sensation is lost while all movement remains normal
cards.explanation: The pyramid carries the corticospinal fibers destined for the lateral tract, so the loss falls hardest on fractionated distal movement, and because the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal pathways run outside the pyramid, they survive and continue to support axial posture. Losing posture while sparing the fingers reverses which pathway was cut. Reflexes are spinal and remain, indeed they become brisk, so nothing is permanently abolished. Sensory pathways lie outside the pyramid and are untouched.

cards.q: What is the cerebellum's main contribution to movement?
cards.a: It compares the intended movement with the actual movement and corrects the error.
options: It supplies the final excitatory drive that reaches the alpha motor neuron
It decides whether a movement should be started at all
It compares the intended movement with the actual movement and corrects the error
It transduces muscle stretch into trains of sensory action potentials
cards.explanation: The cerebellum receives a copy of the descending command and sensory feedback about what the limb actually did, and it uses the mismatch to adjust timing and force, which is why its lesions produce clumsy rather than weak movement. Deciding whether to start a movement is the work of the basal ganglia. Excitatory drive to the alpha motor neuron comes from descending tracts and spinal circuits. Stretch transduction is the job of the muscle spindle.

cards.q: What is the main contribution of the basal ganglia to movement?
cards.a: They help select and initiate wanted movements while suppressing unwanted ones.
options: They generate the walking rhythm used during locomotion
They carry the motor command from the cortex directly down to the spinal cord
They set the sensitivity of the muscle spindle during contraction
They help select and initiate wanted movements while suppressing unwanted ones
cards.explanation: Basal ganglia circuits gate cortical motor output, releasing the movement that was chosen and holding back the competing ones, which is why their disorders show up as too little movement or too much rather than as weakness. The walking rhythm comes from spinal pattern generators. Spindle sensitivity is set by gamma motor neurons. The basal ganglia have no descending spinal projection and act only by way of the thalamus back to cortex.

cards.q: Damage to one cerebellar hemisphere produces motor signs on which side of the body?
cards.a: The same side as the damage.
options: The same side as the damage
The side opposite the damage
Both sides equally
Neither side, since cerebellar damage causes only sensory loss
cards.explanation: Cerebellar output crosses on its way to the thalamus and the corticospinal tract crosses again in the medulla, and two crossings return the influence to the side it started on, so signs are ipsilateral. Contralateral signs are the pattern for lesions of the motor cortex or the corticospinal tract above the decussation. A unilateral lesion does not affect both sides. Cerebellar damage produces incoordination, which is a motor sign, not a loss of sensation.

cards.q: A tremor that is absent at rest and grows worse as the hand approaches a target points to which structure?
cards.a: The cerebellum.
options: The basal ganglia
The cerebellum
The neuromuscular junction
The dorsal columns
cards.explanation: An intention tremor reflects failed online error correction, the cerebellum's specific job, so the oscillation appears only when the movement demands accuracy. Basal ganglia disease classically gives the opposite timing, a tremor present at rest that quiets during movement. Neuromuscular junction disease produces fatigable weakness, not tremor. Dorsal column loss causes clumsiness from lost position sense, which worsens with the eyes closed rather than near a target.

cards.q: Which triad of signs is characteristic of basal ganglia disease of the Parkinson type?
cards.a: Resting tremor, rigidity, and slowness of movement.
options: Flaccid weakness, absent reflexes, and fasciculations
Intention tremor, dysmetria, and a wide based gait
Resting tremor, rigidity, and slowness of movement
Loss of pain sensation, loss of vibration sense, and numbness
cards.explanation: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine reduces the release of selected movements, producing bradykinesia with increased tone and a tremor that appears when the limb is at rest. Intention tremor with dysmetria and a wide based gait is the cerebellar picture. Flaccid weakness with areflexia and fasciculations is a lower motor neuron picture. The sensory list describes a peripheral or spinal sensory lesion and involves no motor system at all.

cards.q: What does dysmetria mean?
cards.a: Misjudging the distance of a movement so the limb overshoots or falls short.
options: Being unable to start a movement at all unless an external cue is given
Losing muscle bulk in the limb over several weeks
Producing involuntary writhing movements at rest
Misjudging the distance of a movement so the limb overshoots or falls short
cards.explanation: Dysmetria is an error in the amplitude of a movement, the finger stopping past the nose or short of it, and it is one of the most reliable cerebellar signs. Trouble starting a movement without a cue is akinesia, a basal ganglia feature. Involuntary writhing at rest describes athetosis, also a basal ganglia sign. Wasting of the limb is a lower motor neuron finding and has nothing to do with coordination.

cards.q: Which pathway supplies dopamine to the striatum?
cards.a: The projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta.
options: The projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta
The projection from the cerebellar dentate nucleus
The projection from the subthalamic nucleus
The projection from the globus pallidus interna
cards.explanation: Dopaminergic cells of the substantia nigra pars compacta send axons to the caudate and putamen, and the death of those cells is what produces Parkinson disease. The subthalamic nucleus is glutamatergic and drives the internal pallidum. The dentate nucleus is cerebellar output and projects to the thalamus. The internal pallidum is the inhibitory output of the basal ganglia and uses GABA, not dopamine.

cards.q: In the basal ganglia, what do the direct and indirect pathways do to movement?
cards.a: The direct pathway facilitates movement and the indirect pathway suppresses it.
options: The direct pathway suppresses movement and the indirect pathway facilitates it
The direct pathway facilitates movement and the indirect pathway suppresses it
Both pathways facilitate movement, differing only in speed
Both pathways suppress movement, differing only in which muscles they reach
cards.explanation: Activity in the direct pathway reduces inhibitory output from the internal pallidum, freeing the thalamus to drive cortex and letting the chosen movement go forward, while the indirect pathway increases that inhibitory output and holds competing movements back. Reversing the two would make dopamine loss cause excess movement rather than bradykinesia. The two pathways are opposed in sign, so describing them as both excitatory or both inhibitory removes the selection function entirely.

cards.q: A stroke damages the right cerebellar hemisphere. On which side would you expect the finger to nose test to be inaccurate?
cards.a: On the right.
options: On both sides equally
On the left
On the right
On neither side, since accuracy does not depend on the cerebellum
cards.explanation: Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the cerebellar output crossing and the corticospinal crossing cancel each other, so a right hemisphere lesion disturbs the right arm. A left sided deficit would follow damage to the right motor cortex instead. Damage on one side does not disturb both arms. Finger to nose accuracy is a direct test of cerebellar error correction, so it is very much affected.

cards.q: A patient's hand is steady while resting in the lap, but it begins to oscillate as she reaches for a cup and the shaking is worst just before she grasps it. Which structure is implicated?
cards.a: The cerebellum.
options: The basal ganglia
The primary motor cortex
The lower motor neuron pool of the forearm
The cerebellum
cards.explanation: The timing is the clue. A tremor that appears only during a goal directed movement and peaks near the target is an intention tremor and reflects failed cerebellar correction of ongoing error. A basal ganglia tremor behaves in the opposite way, present at rest and damped by voluntary movement. A motor cortex lesion produces weakness rather than oscillation. Lower motor neuron damage gives wasting and twitching at rest, not a tremor tied to reaching.

cards.q: A patient's fingers show a slow rhythmic tremor while the hands rest on the knees, and the tremor stops when he picks up a glass. Which structure is implicated?
cards.a: The basal ganglia.
options: The basal ganglia
The cerebellum
The muscle spindle
The dorsal root ganglion
cards.explanation: A tremor that is present at rest and quiets with voluntary movement is the classic basal ganglia pattern seen with nigrostriatal dopamine loss. The cerebellar tremor is the mirror image, absent at rest and worst as the hand nears the target. Spindle malfunction alters reflex gain rather than producing a rhythmic resting tremor. Dorsal root ganglion damage causes sensory loss and sensory clumsiness, not tremor.

cards.q: A patient walks with a wide based, staggering gait and sways badly when standing with the feet together, yet strength and reflexes in the legs are normal. Which structure is most likely involved?
cards.a: The midline cerebellum.
options: The internal capsule
The midline cerebellum
The lateral corticospinal tract
The globus pallidus
cards.explanation: Normal strength and normal reflexes rule out the descending motor pathways, and a wide base with truncal instability points to the midline cerebellum, which coordinates balance and gait. A capsular or corticospinal lesion would leave the leg weak with brisk reflexes. Pallidal disease produces rigidity and slowness or involuntary movements rather than this pattern of unsteadiness with a wide base.

cards.q: If dopamine input to the striatum falls, what happens to the inhibitory output of the internal globus pallidus and to movement?
cards.a: Pallidal inhibitory output rises and movement becomes slow and sparse.
options: Pallidal inhibitory output falls and movement becomes excessive
Pallidal inhibitory output rises and movement becomes excessive
Pallidal inhibitory output rises and movement becomes slow and sparse
Pallidal output is unchanged because dopamine acts only on the cerebellum
cards.explanation: Dopamine normally pushes the direct pathway on and the indirect pathway off, so losing it swings the balance toward the indirect pathway, the internal pallidum fires more, the thalamus is inhibited more, and the cortex receives less drive, which is bradykinesia. Falling pallidal output would release movement, the pattern seen in hyperkinetic disorders. High pallidal output cannot produce excess movement, since more inhibition means less. Dopamine of this system acts on the striatum, not on the cerebellum.

cards.q: A patient has continuous, irregular, dance like movements of the limbs that he cannot suppress. How is this best classified?
cards.a: A hyperkinetic basal ganglia disorder.
options: A lower motor neuron disorder
A hypokinetic basal ganglia disorder
A cerebellar coordination disorder
A hyperkinetic basal ganglia disorder
cards.explanation: Chorea is an excess of unwanted movement, which means the gate that normally suppresses competing movements has been weakened, and that gating belongs to the basal ganglia. A hypokinetic disorder shows the opposite problem, too little movement. Cerebellar disease makes voluntary movement inaccurate but does not generate involuntary movements at rest. Lower motor neuron disease produces weakness and wasting, and its fasciculations are small twitches within a muscle rather than movements of a whole limb.

cards.q: Trace the consequences of losing substantia nigra pars compacta neurons through the basal ganglia circuit to the cortex. Which sequence is correct?
cards.a: Less direct pathway activity and more indirect pathway activity, so more pallidal inhibition of thalamus and less cortical drive.
options: Less direct pathway activity and more indirect pathway activity, so more pallidal inhibition of thalamus and less cortical drive
More direct pathway activity and less indirect pathway activity, so less pallidal inhibition of thalamus and more cortical drive
Less direct pathway activity and less indirect pathway activity, so no net change in thalamic firing
More pallidal inhibition of thalamus, so the corticospinal tract can no longer cross in the medulla
cards.explanation: Dopamine excites the direct pathway through D1 receptors and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2 receptors, so removing it does both harms at once, and the two converge on the same endpoint of a more active internal pallidum. Heavier pallidal inhibition quiets the thalamus, cortex receives less drive, and movement becomes slow and hard to start. The first option describes what a dopamine agonist would do. The third ignores the opposite signs at D1 and D2. The last confuses circuit gain with the anatomical decussation, which is unaffected.

cards.q: After a stroke, a patient overshoots when reaching with the left hand and cannot perform rapid alternating movements with it, but left arm strength and reflexes are normal. Where is the lesion?
cards.a: In the left cerebellar hemisphere.
options: In the right cerebellar hemisphere
In the left cerebellar hemisphere
In the right primary motor cortex
In the left lateral corticospinal tract at C5
cards.explanation: Two inferences are needed. Overshooting and clumsy alternating movements with preserved strength and reflexes identify the problem as cerebellar rather than a descending pathway lesion, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral, so a left sided deficit means a left sided cerebellum. The right cerebellum would disturb the right hand. A right motor cortex lesion or a cervical corticospinal lesion would both produce weakness with brisk reflexes, which is not what the examination shows.

cards.q: Why do cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion even though the cerebellum influences movement through the cerebral cortex?
cards.a: Cerebellar output crosses on the way to the thalamus and the corticospinal tract crosses again, so the influence returns to the starting side.
options: Cerebellar output never crosses the midline at any point
The cerebellum sends its axons straight down the cord to spinal motor neurons on the same side of the body, so no crossing occurs anywhere
Cerebellar output crosses on the way to the thalamus and the corticospinal tract crosses again, so the influence returns to the starting side
The corticospinal tract does not cross in patients who have cerebellar disease
cards.explanation: Count the crossings. Deep cerebellar output leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses to reach the opposite thalamus and motor cortex, and that cortex then sends corticospinal fibers that cross back in the medulla, so two crossings return the effect to the original side. A pathway with no crossing at all would also give ipsilateral signs, but it is not how the anatomy is built. The cerebellum has no direct projection to spinal motor neurons. The pyramidal decussation is fixed anatomy and does not change with disease.

cards.q: A lesion destroys the subthalamic nucleus on one side, and the patient develops violent involuntary flinging movements of the opposite limbs. Why does losing this nucleus increase movement?
cards.a: The subthalamic nucleus drives the internal pallidum, so losing it reduces pallidal inhibition and releases the thalamus.
options: The subthalamic nucleus inhibits the motor cortex directly, so losing it leaves cortical output entirely unopposed
The subthalamic nucleus generates the walking rhythm, so losing it makes the limbs move continuously
The subthalamic nucleus supplies dopamine to the striatum, so losing it mimics Parkinson disease
The subthalamic nucleus drives the internal pallidum, so losing it reduces pallidal inhibition and releases the thalamus
cards.explanation: The subthalamic nucleus is the excitatory relay of the indirect pathway onto the internal pallidum, so removing it weakens the brake: pallidal firing falls, the thalamus is disinhibited, and cortex drives far more movement than intended. The nucleus does not project to cortex directly, so an unopposed cortex is the wrong mechanism. Dopamine comes from the substantia nigra pars compacta, and losing dopamine would slow movement rather than release it. Locomotor rhythm is generated in the spinal cord.

cards.q: Which neuron is the lower motor neuron?
cards.a: The ventral horn cell whose axon leaves the cord and reaches the muscle.
options: The ventral horn cell whose axon leaves the cord and reaches the muscle
The cortical cell whose axon descends to the spinal cord
The dorsal root ganglion cell that carries stretch information inward
The spinal interneuron that connects one side of the cord to the other
cards.explanation: The lower motor neuron is the cell that actually contacts skeletal muscle, so its cell body sits in the ventral horn of the cord or in a cranial nerve motor nucleus and its axon runs out in a peripheral nerve. The cortical cell that descends to the cord is the upper motor neuron and stops in the spinal gray matter. Dorsal root ganglion cells are sensory. Interneurons stay inside the central nervous system and never reach muscle.

cards.q: What happens to muscle tone after an upper motor neuron lesion?
cards.a: Tone increases, producing spasticity.
options: Tone falls, producing flaccidity
Tone increases, producing spasticity
Tone is unchanged from normal
Tone rises for a day and then falls permanently
cards.explanation: Descending pathways normally restrain the spinal stretch reflex, so removing them leaves the reflex circuitry overactive and the limb resists passive stretch, which is spasticity. Flaccidity is the tone change of a lower motor neuron lesion, where the reflex arc itself is broken. Tone does change, and durably, so unchanged tone does not fit. The time course given in the last option is backwards: tone is low at first after an acute lesion and rises over the following weeks.

cards.q: What happens to muscle tone after a lower motor neuron lesion?
cards.a: Tone falls, and the muscle becomes flaccid.
options: Tone increases, and the muscle becomes spastic
Tone is normal, but only during voluntary effort
Tone falls, and the muscle becomes flaccid
Tone alternates between high and low from minute to minute
cards.explanation: Cutting the final common pathway removes the only route by which any excitation, voluntary or reflex, can reach the muscle, so the muscle goes limp. Spasticity requires an intact spinal reflex arc released from descending control, which is the upper motor neuron picture. Tone is a resting property and does not become normal only during effort. Fluctuating tone is not a feature of a denervated muscle.

cards.q: What happens to deep tendon reflexes after an upper motor neuron lesion has been present for several weeks?
cards.a: They become exaggerated.
options: They disappear completely
They can be elicited only with the eyes closed
They stay exactly normal
They become exaggerated
cards.explanation: The spinal reflex arc survives an upper motor neuron lesion and loses the descending inhibition that normally damps it, so tendon taps produce brisk responses and sometimes clonus. Reflexes disappear when the arc itself is interrupted, which is the lower motor neuron pattern. Normal reflexes would mean descending control was still intact. Eye closure is a maneuver used to reinforce a reflex, not a requirement created by the lesion.

cards.q: What happens to deep tendon reflexes after a lower motor neuron lesion?
cards.a: They are reduced or absent.
options: They are reduced or absent
They are exaggerated, with clonus
They are normal, since the reflex needs no motor neuron
They are replaced by an extensor plantar response
cards.explanation: The lower motor neuron is the efferent limb of the tendon reflex, so damaging it breaks the arc and the tap produces little or no contraction. Brisk reflexes with clonus are the upper motor neuron picture, where the arc is intact but unrestrained. The reflex certainly needs a motor neuron, since without one nothing can reach the muscle. An extensor plantar response is a separate upper motor neuron sign, not a substitute reflex.

cards.q: What is a Babinski sign?
cards.a: Extension of the great toe when the sole of the foot is stroked.
options: Rapid rhythmic beating of the foot when the ankle is dorsiflexed
Extension of the great toe when the sole of the foot is stroked
Small twitches visible under the skin of a resting muscle
Loss of the ability to feel the sole of the foot being touched
cards.explanation: Stroking the sole normally makes the toes curl downward, and an upgoing great toe instead indicates loss of corticospinal control, which makes the Babinski sign an upper motor neuron sign. Rhythmic beating at the ankle is clonus, which is also an upper motor neuron sign but a different one. Twitches in a resting muscle are fasciculations and point to the lower motor neuron. Loss of sensation on the sole is a sensory finding and says nothing about motor level.

cards.q: Fasciculations, the small visible twitches in a muscle at rest, indicate damage at which level?
cards.a: The lower motor neuron.
options: The upper motor neuron
The cerebellum
The lower motor neuron
The sensory afferent fiber
cards.explanation: A fasciculation is the spontaneous discharge of a single injured motor unit, so it requires a sick or dying lower motor neuron and its muscle fibers. Upper motor neuron lesions leave the motor unit intact and produce spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign instead. Cerebellar disease affects coordination and produces no spontaneous twitching. Sensory fiber damage causes numbness or tingling and cannot make a muscle fiber contract.

cards.q: How does muscle bulk differ between upper and lower motor neuron lesions?
cards.a: Atrophy is marked in a lower motor neuron lesion and slight in an upper motor neuron lesion.
options: Atrophy is marked in an upper motor neuron lesion and slight in a lower motor neuron lesion
Muscle bulk is preserved in both, since neither affects the muscle itself
Atrophy is equally severe in both, since both cause weakness
Atrophy is marked in a lower motor neuron lesion and slight in an upper motor neuron lesion
cards.explanation: Denervation strips the muscle of both its activity and the trophic support of its motor neuron, so a lower motor neuron lesion wastes the muscle quickly and severely. After an upper motor neuron lesion the muscle keeps its innervation and its reflex activity, so any wasting is mild, late, and mostly from disuse. Reversing the two contradicts that mechanism. Weakness alone does not determine bulk, which is why the two lesions differ despite both causing weakness.

cards.q: A limb is flaccid and markedly wasted, the tendon reflexes are absent, and twitches are visible in the muscle at rest. Which level is damaged?
cards.a: The lower motor neuron.
options: The lower motor neuron
The upper motor neuron
The cerebellum
The basal ganglia
cards.explanation: All four findings point the same way: low tone, absent reflexes, severe wasting, and fasciculations are exactly what happens when the final common pathway to the muscle is destroyed. An upper motor neuron lesion would give the opposite tone and reflexes, spasticity and hyperreflexia, along with a Babinski sign and little wasting. Cerebellar disease causes incoordination with normal strength and bulk. Basal ganglia disease alters the amount of movement rather than abolishing reflexes or wasting the muscle.

cards.q: A limb is weak and stiff, the tendon reflexes are brisk, the great toe goes up when the sole is stroked, and muscle bulk is nearly normal. Which level is damaged?
cards.a: The upper motor neuron.
options: The lower motor neuron
The upper motor neuron
The neuromuscular junction
The muscle fibers themselves
cards.explanation: Increased tone, hyperreflexia, an extensor plantar response, and preserved bulk are the four features of an upper motor neuron lesion, and they occur together because the spinal reflex machinery survives and is released from descending control. A lower motor neuron lesion would show flaccidity, lost reflexes, fasciculations, and obvious wasting. Neuromuscular junction disease causes fatigable weakness with normal or reduced reflexes and no Babinski sign. Primary muscle disease weakens and wastes muscle without making reflexes brisk.

cards.q: A herniated disc compresses the L5 ventral root. Which set of findings is expected in the muscles that root supplies?
cards.a: Flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes, fasciculations, and wasting over time.
options: Spastic weakness with brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response on that side
Normal strength with loss of coordination and an intention tremor
Flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes, fasciculations, and wasting over time
Weakness that worsens through the day and recovers fully with rest
cards.explanation: The ventral root carries the axons of lower motor neurons, so compressing it is a lower motor neuron lesion and produces the flaccid, areflexic, wasting picture with fasciculations in the affected myotome. Spasticity with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe requires a lesion of descending pathways in the brain or cord, not of a root. Coordination problems with intention tremor point to the cerebellum. Fatigable weakness that recovers with rest is the pattern of neuromuscular junction disease.

cards.q: A patient has an infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Two months later, which pattern is expected in the affected arm?
cards.a: Increased tone, brisk reflexes, an extensor plantar response, and little wasting.
options: Increased tone, absent reflexes, and severe wasting
Decreased tone, absent reflexes, visible fasciculations, and severe wasting
Normal tone and reflexes with inaccurate reaching
Increased tone, brisk reflexes, an extensor plantar response, and little wasting
cards.explanation: The capsule carries upper motor neuron axons, so interrupting them leaves the spinal arc intact but unrestrained, and after the acute phase the arm shows spasticity, hyperreflexia, a Babinski sign, and preserved bulk. The flaccid areflexic set with fasciculations belongs to a lower motor neuron lesion. Normal tone and reflexes with inaccurate reaching is the cerebellar pattern. High tone with absent reflexes is internally inconsistent, since spasticity is produced by the very reflex arc that would have to be broken for reflexes to vanish.

cards.q: Why is muscle wasting so much more severe after a lower motor neuron lesion than after an upper motor neuron lesion?
cards.a: The muscle loses its innervation entirely, along with the activity and trophic support the motor neuron provides.
options: The muscle loses its innervation entirely, along with the activity and trophic support the motor neuron provides
The muscle loses its blood supply, because the artery feeding it runs alongside the motor axon in the nerve
Upper motor neuron lesions cause the muscle to grow rather than shrink
Lower motor neuron lesions dissolve the tendon that anchors the muscle
cards.explanation: Denervated fibers receive no activation at all and also lose the trophic influence of their motor neuron, so protein breakdown outpaces synthesis and the muscle wastes rapidly. After an upper motor neuron lesion the motor neuron still fires in reflexes and still supports its fibers, so bulk is largely maintained. Blood supply travels with vessels and is not lost with the motor axon. Upper motor neuron lesions do not cause muscle growth, and tendons are not dissolved by denervation.

cards.q: A healthy four month old infant shows an upgoing great toe when the sole is stroked. What is the best interpretation?
cards.a: It is a normal finding at this age, because corticospinal myelination is incomplete.
options: It shows that a lower motor neuron lesion is present in the nerves supplying the leg
It is a normal finding at this age, because corticospinal myelination is incomplete
It proves a cerebellar lesion is present
It means the infant has lost sensation in the sole of the foot
cards.explanation: The downgoing plantar response depends on mature corticospinal control, and that control develops over the first year or two, so an extensor response in an infant is expected and not a sign of disease. In an adult the same response is an upper motor neuron sign, which is a good example of the same finding meaning different things at different ages. It is never a lower motor neuron sign, since those are flaccidity, lost reflexes, fasciculations, and wasting. It is a motor reflex response and does not indicate cerebellar damage or sensory loss.

cards.q: A patient has visible tongue fasciculations and wasted hand muscles, and at the same time the knee reflexes are very brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. What does this combination indicate?
cards.a: Both upper and lower motor neurons are affected.
options: Only the lower motor neuron is affected, and the brisk reflexes are a normal variant
Only the upper motor neuron is affected, and the wasting is from disuse alone
Both upper and lower motor neurons are affected
Neither motor level is affected, since the findings contradict each other
cards.explanation: Sort the findings by level. Fasciculations and marked wasting can only come from lower motor neuron damage, while brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses can only come from upper motor neuron damage, so both levels must be involved. Calling the brisk reflexes a normal variant ignores the extensor plantars, which are not normal in an adult. Disuse atrophy does not produce fasciculations. The findings do not contradict each other; they are in different regions and simply point to disease at two levels at once.

cards.q: A cord lesion destroys the ventral horn at C6 on the left and also cuts the descending tracts at that level. Months later, what is expected in the left biceps at C6 and in the left leg?
cards.a: The biceps is wasted and flaccid with a lost reflex, while the leg is spastic with brisk reflexes.
options: The biceps is spastic with brisk reflexes, while the leg is flaccid and wasted
Both the biceps and the leg are wasted and flaccid, with reflexes lost in the arm and the leg alike
Both the biceps and the leg are spastic with brisk reflexes
The biceps is wasted and flaccid with a lost reflex, while the leg is spastic with brisk reflexes
cards.explanation: Two mechanisms operate at once. At the level of the lesion the lower motor neurons themselves are gone, so those muscles show the flaccid, wasted, areflexic picture, while below the level the lower motor neurons survive but lose descending control, so those segments show spasticity and hyperreflexia. Flaccidity everywhere would require destruction of motor neurons at every segment. Spasticity everywhere ignores the destroyed C6 ventral horn. The last option reverses the two zones and puts the lower motor neuron signs below rather than at the lesion.

cards.q: Immediately after an acute spinal cord injury, the limbs below the lesion are flaccid and all reflexes are absent, yet weeks later the same limbs are spastic and hyperreflexic. How is this explained?
cards.a: Spinal circuits are temporarily depressed after the injury and later recover, revealing the release from descending control.
options: Spinal circuits are temporarily depressed after the injury and later recover, revealing the release from descending control
The lower motor neurons below the injury died at first and then regenerated over the following weeks, restoring the reflexes
The lesion moved from the lower motor neuron level to the upper motor neuron level
The descending tracts regrew across the injury and restored excess tone
cards.explanation: The lesion was an upper motor neuron lesion the whole time. Acutely, the sudden loss of descending drive leaves spinal neurons below the injury profoundly unexcitable, a state called spinal shock, so the limbs look flaccid and areflexic and can be mistaken for a lower motor neuron problem. As those circuits regain excitability over days to weeks, the intact reflex arcs are unmasked without their descending restraint and the expected spasticity and hyperreflexia appear. Lower motor neurons neither died nor regenerated, the lesion did not move, and severed descending tracts do not regrow across the injury.

cards.q: A patient has a wasted calf with visible fasciculations, an absent ankle reflex, reduced tone in the foot, and a downgoing plantar response. Which single site of damage fits all of these findings?
cards.a: The S1 ventral root.
options: The lateral corticospinal tract at T10
The S1 ventral root
The posterior limb of the internal capsule
The primary motor cortex leg area
cards.explanation: Every finding here is a lower motor neuron finding: wasting, fasciculations, an absent reflex, and low tone, and the downgoing plantar response actively argues against upper motor neuron involvement. Only a lesion of the motor axons leaving the cord fits, and the S1 root supplies the calf and carries the ankle reflex. The corticospinal tract at T10, the internal capsule, and the motor cortex leg area are all upper motor neuron sites, and each would produce spasticity, brisk reflexes, an upgoing toe, and preserved bulk instead.
